why: The Munger judge's ranked fix: 'urgency is a choice' has no counterweight for chronically missed timelines. These are human-authored, public-record fact atoms (claim_type=fact, verification=verified, proof_ref=dated statements) so the brain can invert on its own overconfidence instead of only celebrating it. Not gotchas — the calibration record.

atoms.content: In October 2016, Musk announced that a Tesla would drive itself coast-to-coast — Los Angeles to New York — 'by the end of next year' (2017) with no human intervention. The demonstration never took place, in 2017 or any year since.
atoms.implication: Musk's urgency doctrine produces real velocity and real schedule misses from the same mechanism. When applying his 'deadlines are targets to compress' pattern, budget for the documented gap between his announced timelines and delivery.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Tesla Autopilot 2.0 announcement, October 19, 2016
atoms.proof_ref: Oct 2016 Tesla HW2 press call ('by the end of next year… from a parking lot in California to a parking lot in New York'); no such demo has occurred

atoms.content: At Tesla Autonomy Day in April 2019, Musk predicted 'over a million robotaxis on the road' by the end of 2020, telling investors he felt 'very confident' about the timeline. No Tesla robotaxi operated commercially in 2020; a limited supervised robotaxi pilot did not launch until 2025.
atoms.implication: His most confident public timelines have been the least reliable — confidence level is not a calibration signal in his forecasts. Weight his 'physics says it's possible' arguments separately from his 'when' claims; the first has a far better record than the second.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Tesla Autonomy Day, April 22, 2019
atoms.proof_ref: Autonomy Day webcast, Apr 2019 ('a million robotaxis on the road' by end of 2020); Austin supervised pilot began June 2025

atoms.content: Musk publicly predicted full self-driving would arrive roughly 'next year' nearly every year from 2014 through 2022 — including 'full autonomy in about two years' (2015), 'feature complete this year' (2019), and 'I'm extremely confident of achieving full autonomy… this year' (2021, 2022). Unsupervised full self-driving was not achieved in any of those years.
atoms.implication: This is the single most repeated timeline miss in his public record — a decade of one-year-out predictions for the same milestone. Any reasoning in his voice about imminent technology breakthroughs should carry this base rate.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: compiled FSD timeline statements, 2014-2022
atoms.proof_ref: Documented yearly statements: 2015 Fortune interview; 2016 'two years' (Recode); 2019 Autonomy Day 'feature complete'; 2021/2022 earnings calls

atoms.content: At the 2016 IAC in Guadalajara, Musk presented a Mars architecture with cargo flights beginning in 2022 and crewed flights in 2024. Neither occurred; no Starship has flown to Mars as of 2026.
atoms.implication: His Mars timelines compress physics-limited and organization-limited work into the same optimistic schedule. The vision has held for two decades — the dates have never held. Cite the mission, hedge the calendar.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: IAC Guadalajara presentation, September 27, 2016
atoms.proof_ref: IAC 2016 'Making Humans a Multiplanetary Species' (cargo 2022, crew 2024); SpaceX launch record through 2026

atoms.content: The second-generation Tesla Roadster was unveiled in November 2017 with production stated for 2020 and $50,000 reservations taken. As of 2026 it has not shipped — six-plus years past the announced date.
atoms.implication: Product announcements with paid reservations are still schedule-optimistic in his system. The pattern: announcement dates serve recruiting, morale, and capital — delivery dates are downstream of engineering reality he does not pretend to fully control.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Tesla Semi/Roadster unveil event, November 16, 2017
atoms.proof_ref: Nov 2017 unveil (production '2020'); no customer deliveries as of 2026

atoms.content: In mid-2017 Musk targeted Model 3 production of 5,000 cars per week by the end of 2017. Tesla did not reach that rate until roughly July 2018 — more than six months late, through a period Musk himself called 'production hell' and 'the most difficult and painful year of my career.'
atoms.implication: Even his manufacturing-ramp promises — the domain where he is strongest — run materially late under first-of-kind complexity. His own description of the cost ('sleeping on the factory floor') is the honest counterweight to the schedule bravado.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Tesla Q2 2017 guidance; Q2 2018 production report
atoms.proof_ref: Tesla 2017 guidance (5k/week by end 2017) vs. ~5,031/week first achieved week ending July 1, 2018; 'production hell' — Musk, multiple 2017-18 statements

atoms.content: The Cybertruck was unveiled in November 2019 with production announced for late 2021. First customer deliveries came in November 2023 — about two years late.
atoms.implication: A two-year slip on a headline consumer product is his normal error bar, not a crisis. Calibrate any 'shipping next year' claim in his voice against this distribution.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Cybertruck unveil November 21, 2019; first deliveries November 30, 2023
atoms.proof_ref: Unveil event (production 'late 2021') vs. delivery event Nov 30, 2023

atoms.content: At TED in April 2022, pressed by Chris Anderson on years of missed full-self-driving predictions, Musk acknowledged the pattern himself: 'I'm the boy who cried FSD' — while maintaining the goal was still achievable.
atoms.implication: He is aware of his own timeline miscalibration and jokes about it without changing the behavior — the optimism is a chosen operating stance, not an information gap. A faithful model of his reasoning must carry both: the self-awareness and the refusal to recalibrate.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: TED 2022 interview with Chris Anderson, April 14, 2022

atoms.content: In 2011, Musk said he expected to put a human on Mars within 10 to 15 years — i.e., by roughly 2021-2026. As of 2026 no human has traveled to Mars, and no crewed Mars mission has launched.
atoms.implication: His longest-horizon predictions miss by the widest margins, yet they are also the ones that recruited the teams and capital that made the underlying capability real. The productive reading: his dates are instruments of mobilization, not forecasts — treat them accordingly.
atoms.source_ref: Public record: Wall Street Journal interview, April 2011
atoms.proof_ref: WSJ 'The Wall Street Journal Report' Apr 2011 ('I'm confident… 10 years, maybe 15'); no crewed Mars mission as of 2026
